searched: Read _backend-system/README.md (confirms LAW.md/RATIONALE.md/AUDIT/QUESTIONS.md do not exist yet, research/ and audit/ folders exist without a trust-specific topic), _rules/KEY_FEATURES.md, _tasks/REFUND_APPEAL_PLAN.md (full, including the 2026-06-01 council verdict sections 10-14), app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx (the full written ToS, all 15 sections), lib/automod.ts, lib/strikes.ts, lib/cancellation-policy.ts, lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts, lib/bookings/charge-fee.ts, app/api/reviews/route.ts, app/api/reviews/eligibility/route.ts, app/api/admin/reviews/[id]/route.ts, app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts, app/api/salon/documents/route.ts, app/api/auth/verify-phone/check/route.ts, app/api/salons/route.ts (POST/onboarding, lines 630-700), app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (dispute.created/closed handlers), lib/validations.ts (salonPolicyUpdateSchema, booking_disputes reason enums, content-reports reasons), lib/content-reports.ts, _design-system/PSYCHOLOGY.md (review-trust laws), _design-system/REMOVED.md (checked for graveyarded trust features, found the dead salon-verification edge function and the dead reviews/homepage endpoint). Ran targeted greps for: chargeback, dispute, refund policy, no-show, fraud, verification, onboarding, kyc, fake/duplicate listing, harassment, mediation, account_warnings (read call sites), phone_verified, across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md, both hooks directories, and the live app/lib tree, each recorded per-finding below. Did not query the live DB (no MCP write/read access used); relied on _docs/BACKEND.md's live-verified claims plus my own static reads of the actual route/lib files, which is stronger evidence than the docs alone.

findings.title: Salon phone verification is a silent no-op: promised in the ToS, faked by the code
findings.principle: Any account attribute the Terms of Service represent to users as verified (phone, email, business identity) must be written to the database by the same request that confirms it, and no admin approval action may activate an account while that field is still false. A verification endpoint that returns `verified:true` without persisting a corresponding DB write is a defect, not a deferred feature, and ships blocked until fixed.
findings.why: Users and salon partners read `verified` badges and ToS promises as a factual claim about safety. If the code that is supposed to make the claim true instead simulates success and quietly skips the write, the platform is asserting something false to every customer who trusts a verified salon, and the founder has no record of what was actually checked if a dispute or fraud case ever needs it.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/auth/verify-phone/check/route.ts:56-63: the OTP check succeeds, deletes the Redis code, and returns `{verified:true}` with a comment admitting 'They will do that in the POST /api/salons handler when they submit the form.' app/api/salons/route.ts:696 is that handler, and the write is commented out: `// phone_verified: phone_verified || false, // [FIX] Bypassing schema cache error (defaults to false in DB)`. Also app/api/auth/verify-phone/check/route.ts:35-38: when UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL/TOKEN are unset, the endpoint returns 'Verifiziert (Simuliert - Redis fehlt)' for ANY code, no OTP check at all. Separately, app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts:24-37 (the admin approve action) never reads phone_verified or salon_documents at all before setting `is_active:true`, so even a correctly-written phone_verified would not currently gate activation.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "phone_verified" app lib --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx | grep -v database.types.ts -> 3 hits total: the schema field, the destructure, and the commented-out write. grep -n "phone_verified\|salon_documents" app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts -> zero hits, confirming the approval action reads neither.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx:49-52 (ToS §2.4) explicitly promises 'Salon Partners must verify their email address and phone number before their account is activated,' and lib/database.types.ts models a phone_verified column, but nothing in the runtime path ever sets it true or reads it before activation.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md under authn (a new 'verification claims must be truthful' row) + a fix to app/api/salons/route.ts and app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts
findings.enforcement: gate: a CI/pre-deploy check that greps for any endpoint returning `verified:true`/`{ok:true}` alongside a commented-out DB write in the same diff hunk is too fragile to automate reliably; the practical enforcement is a code-review checklist item ('every verification success path has a corresponding persisted write, proven by a passing integration test') plus fixing this specific instance now, since it is live-broken, not merely undocumented.

findings.title: Per-salon cancellation/no-show fee has no code ceiling matching the ToS-promised platform cap
findings.principle: Every per-salon policy value that the Terms of Service describe as bounded by a platform-wide standard (here: cancellation fee <= 50% and free-cancellation window >= 24h before the appointment) must be validated server-side against that exact numeric ceiling at write time, not just against an internal sanity bound like 'percentage <= 100'. If the ToS number and the validation ceiling ever diverge, the ToS text is the one to change, not the other way around, and the change follows the ToS-amendment notice process in the same document.
findings.why: A marketplace's written cancellation/no-show terms are the one promise customers rely on before entering a card. If any individual salon can quietly set a stricter policy than what every customer was told applies platform-wide, the platform is exposed to a straightforward Swiss consumer-protection and false-advertising claim the moment real money starts moving, and it erodes exactly the trust the two-sided marketplace depends on.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx:92-100 (ToS §4.2-4.3): late cancellation fee is fixed at 50% platform-wide, and 'terms may not be stricter than the platform standards' (implying a ceiling on the free-cancel window at 24h and the fee at 50%). lib/validations.ts:949-964 (salonPolicyUpdateSchema) only caps a PERCENTAGE type at <=100 (its own self-consistency bound, 'you can never charge more than the customer paid') and caps free_cancel_hours between 1 and 168 -- there is no comparison anywhere in the schema or in lib/cancellation-policy.ts against the ToS's 50% or 24h figures. A salon can legally save cancellation_fee_type='percentage', cancellation_fee_value=100, free_cancel_hours=1 today, meaning a customer cancelling 20 hours out (well inside the ToS's promised free-cancel window) gets charged the full booking value.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "50\|24" lib/cancellation-policy.ts lib/validations.ts (salonPolicyUpdateSchema block, lines 946-964) -> no reference to 50 or 24 anywhere in the fee-calculation or validation code; the only cap present is the 100%-of-paid fairness cap, which is a different and weaker constraint than the ToS ceiling. grep -rn "platform standard\|platform-wide\|ceiling\|max.*fee" lib/cancellation-policy.ts -> zero hits.
findings.existing_coverage: none in code; the constraint exists only as ToS prose (§4.2-4.3) with no corresponding server-side check.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md under api-design or a new marketplace-trust topic; enforced in lib/validations.ts salonPolicyUpdateSchema (reject cancellation_fee_value>50 for type='percentage' unless a documented salon-leniency exception applies, and free_cancel_hours<24)
findings.enforcement: gate: extend the zod refine() on salonPolicyUpdateSchema to hard-cap cancellation_fee_value<=50 (percentage) and free_cancel_hours>=24, with a unit test asserting a 100%-fee/1-hour-window payload is rejected with 400

findings.title: account_warnings is write-only: the ToS's promised strike/suspension consequences never fire
findings.principle: A moderation signal that the Terms of Service promise will produce a consequence (warning email, demotion, suspension) must have a reader, not just a writer. Every INSERT into a penalty/strike table needs a corresponding scheduled job or gate that (a) surfaces the row to a human queue or (b) automatically applies the stated consequence, and this pairing is verified in the same PR that adds the writer.
findings.why: Writing a severity='suspension' row that nothing ever reads is worse than not tracking strikes at all: it creates a false sense that repeat no-show or cancellation abuse is handled, while the actual behavior (nothing happens) diverges completely from both the ToS text and the founder's mental model of the system. A customer with 8 no-shows in 6 months is, today, in exactly the same standing as a customer with zero.
findings.local_evidence: lib/strikes.ts:1-92 (evaluateBookingPenalties, explicitly comment-tagged 'ToS §3.3' and 'ToS §4.4') inserts account_warnings rows with severity warning/strike/suspension whenever a customer hits 3 or 5+ no-shows in 6 months, or a salon hits 3+ cancellations in 30 days. grep across the whole app/ and lib/ trees for any SELECT from account_warnings, outside the generated database.types.ts, returns zero results: no cron, no admin dashboard page, no booking-creation gate, nothing checks this table. profiles.is_suspended / banned_at and salons.frozen_at are never set as a consequence of an account_warnings row.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn "account_warnings" app lib --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx | grep -v database.types.ts -> only lib/strikes.ts (3 .insert() call sites). grep -rln "account_warnings" app lib -> lib/strikes.ts and lib/database.types.ts only, confirming zero reader files exist anywhere in the codebase.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the WRITER exists and even self-documents the ToS section it implements (lib/strikes.ts comments cite '§3.3' and '§4.4' verbatim), but the promised consequence side is completely unbuilt; this is the exact 'code implements an unwritten (here: half-written) policy' shape the probe asked about, inverted -- the policy IS written (in the ToS), the code claims to implement it, but silently doesn't finish the job.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md under a new marketplace-trust or reliability topic ('every strike writer needs a strike reader'); implementation: an admin queue reading account_warnings by severity, plus a cron or booking-creation check that blocks new bookings for severity='suspension' users
findings.enforcement: gate: a small script asserting every table name ending in _warnings, _strikes, or _flags that appears in an .insert() call somewhere in app/lib also appears in at least one .select() call somewhere else in app/lib; fails today for account_warnings specifically

findings.title: No refund/appeal reporting window exists in writing or in code, leaving indefinite reopenable liability
findings.principle: A marketplace's refund/complaint policy must state a maximum number of days after service delivery during which a customer may open a money-back case, and the booking_disputes creation endpoint must enforce that window server-side (reject a new case opened outside it, absent a documented exception like a chargeback). Pick the number once, write it in the ToS, and make the code match it exactly.
findings.why: Without a stated window, every completed booking stays an open financial liability forever: a salon can never treat a booking's revenue as final, payouts can never be confidently reconciled, and Solen (as Merchant of Record) carries indefinite refund risk on money it already passed through. Uber's 48h and most EU marketplaces' 14-30 day windows exist precisely to bound this.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §13.1 (lines 388-391) only says solen.ch 'provides a channel for reporting issues' with no deadline anywhere in the document. _tasks/REFUND_APPEAL_PLAN.md section 11 (lines 201-211) explicitly flags this as still open: 'Reporting window: a customer can open a refund case up to N days after the appointment (Uber uses 48h; proposed default 14 days for appointments, owner to confirm)' -- and that plan is dated 2026-06-01, roughly 8 weeks stale as of the current date with no resolution found. lib/validations.ts:975-984 (the refund-request schema) has no date/window check at all; app/api/bookings/[id]/dispute or the booking_disputes creation route was not found to check booking.starts_at or completed_at against any cutoff.
findings.absence_proof: grep -in "reporting window\|N days\|14 days\|48h\|statute of limitations\|Frist.*Rückerstattung" app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx _tasks/REFUND_APPEAL_PLAN.md lib/validations.ts -> only the one unresolved mention inside REFUND_APPEAL_PLAN.md §11; zero mentions in the shipped ToS or in the validation schema.
findings.existing_coverage: none: this is a genuinely open owner decision, already correctly identified internally, just never closed and never written into the shipped ToS or enforced in code.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §13 (add a stated window) + lib/validations.ts refund-request schema (enforce it) + _backend-system/LAW.md
findings.enforcement: gate: reject a POST to the refund/appeal-creation route when now() - booking.starts_at exceeds the configured window (e.g. 14 days), tested with a case exactly 1 day past the cutoff

findings.title: Salon business-identity verification is entirely optional and never gates activation; no written manual-review checklist exists either
findings.principle: At this scale (~28 salons, pre-launch, one-person manual admin approval), full automated KYC/business verification is premature machinery and should NOT be built now. What IS due now, at zero engineering cost, is a one-page written checklist of exactly what the admin looks at before clicking 'Approve' (e.g. commercial-register lookup by name+address, a phone call, matching the submitted address to a real storefront), because that checklist is what protects the platform's credibility and is what an admin approve action should visibly reference. The trigger for building real automated verification (document-status gating the approve endpoint, a required document type) is: the platform stops manually vetting every single new salon one at a time, which typically happens once new-salon signups exceed roughly 5-10 per week or the founder is no longer personally approving each one.
findings.why: Right now nothing distinguishes 'the founder eyeballed this business and it's real' from 'someone clicked approve.' A written checklist costs nothing and creates an auditable trail; skipping it means the platform cannot later show what due diligence was performed if a fraudulent salon causes harm to a customer, and there is no way to know today whether the manual process is even consistent between the person doing it and any future hire.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/salon/documents/route.ts:23-72 lets a salon owner upload trade_license/professional_cert/hygiene_cert/id_proof/address_proof documents with status:'pending', but app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts:24-37 never selects from salon_documents, never checks a document status, and approves purely on an admin clicking a button -- the upload system and the approval decision are two disconnected systems. app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §6.2 (lines 165-168) itself says proof 'is currently not mandatory for activation.'
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "salon_documents" app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts app/api/admin/salons/route.ts -> zero hits in either. grep -rn "checklist\|manual review\|admin.*verif" _rules _docs/BACKEND.md _backend-system -> no written admin-side verification checklist found anywhere.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the document-upload plumbing exists and the ToS is honest that proof isn't mandatory yet, but there is zero written procedure for what the admin actually checks, and the one dead salon-verification Supabase edge function found in _design-system/REMOVED.md:65 confirms an earlier, abandoned attempt at automating this that was never replaced with either automation or a documented manual process.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new short doc, e.g. _backend-system/audit/salon-onboarding.md or a QUESTIONS.md entry, plus a one-line addition to the admin approve UI showing the checklist inline
findings.enforcement: checklist (not a gate at this scale): a fixed markdown list the admin reads before every approve click; revisit as a code gate (require salon_documents.status='approved' before is_active=true) only once the volume trigger above is hit

findings.title: No differentiated safety/harassment report category exists, so the ToS's 'zero-tolerance, immediate suspension' promise has no trigger
findings.principle: Any report or dispute-reason taxonomy used by a marketplace that promises 'zero tolerance' and 'immediate suspension' for harassment, discrimination, or threats (in either direction, customer-to-staff or salon-to-customer) must include a distinct reason code for exactly that category, and that code must route to a priority queue distinct from ordinary billing/quality complaints, because a promise of immediate action requires a signal fast enough to act on immediately.
findings.why: Today a harassment report and a 'the price was wrong' complaint land in the same bucket with the same non-urgent handling. A marketplace that explicitly promises zero tolerance for abusive behavior toward salon staff (and implicitly needs the same protection for customers) cannot deliver on that promise if the only way anyone learns about a safety incident is an admin happening to read a generic 'other' complaint and recognizing its severity themselves.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §7.3 (lines 231-234): 'solen.ch maintains a zero-tolerance policy for abusive behavior by Customers toward salon staff... will result in immediate account suspension'; §12.2 lists harassment as immediate-termination grounds. lib/validations.ts:742 (booking_disputes issue_type enum) = ['quality','no_show_by_salon','wrong_service','overcharge','other'] and lib/content-reports.ts:70 (REPORT_REASONS) = ['inappropriate','spam','fake','ip_violation','other'] -- neither taxonomy has a harassment/safety/threat code, and there is no salon-side 'report this customer' endpoint at all (only booking-level complaint routes were found).
findings.absence_proof: grep -in "harassment\|safety.*incident\|threat\|abuse" lib/validations.ts lib/content-reports.ts -> zero hits in either enum definition. grep -rln "report.*customer\|reportCustomer\|flag.*customer" app/api lib -> zero results, confirming no salon-initiated report-a-customer path exists.
findings.existing_coverage: none in the taxonomy; the ToS promise exists in prose only, with no code path that can distinguish this case from a routine complaint.
findings.where_it_should_live: lib/validations.ts (add 'harassment' to both the booking_disputes issue_type enum and content-reports REPORT_REASONS) + an admin queue priority flag
findings.enforcement: gate: none needed beyond the schema addition; behaviorally, an admin-queue sort that surfaces reason='harassment' rows first is the practical enforcement

findings.title: No written policy for who absorbs a refund shortfall when a salon's Connect balance can't cover the clawback
findings.principle: State explicitly, in a document the founder can point to, what happens when a refund is approved for a booking whose payout has already reached the salon's bank account and the salon's Stripe Connect balance is insufficient to reverse the transfer: does Solen front the money and invoice the salon, does the refund queue until the salon's balance recovers, or does Solen deduct it from the salon's NEXT payout automatically. Pick one, write it down, and make the code's failure-handling match it (it does not today, beyond throwing a generic error).
findings.why: This is not a hypothetical: the platform pays out weekly with only a 7-day hold (ToS §5.4), so any refund approved in week 2 for a week-1 booking is guaranteed to hit an already-paid-out balance. Without a stated policy, the actual behavior in that moment is whatever the on-call engineer decides at 2am, which is exactly the 'training memory decides' failure mode the backend-system folder exists to prevent, just for money instead of code style.
findings.local_evidence: lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts:173-184 sets reverse_transfer:true and refund_application_fee on every Connect refund, and the file's own comment at line 214 references 'insufficient platform balance' as a known Stripe failure mode the code catches and surfaces as an error -- but catching the error is not the same as having a policy for what happens next to the customer's money. app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx has no section addressing this; §5.4 (payouts) and §5.5 (refunds) are both silent on the interaction between the two. _tasks/REFUND_APPEAL_PLAN.md §7 (line 102) names this exact risk in 2026-06-01 and it remains unresolved: 'Need the Connect model... and a policy for who absorbs post-payout refunds. Classic marketplace risk.'
findings.absence_proof: grep -in "insufficient.*balance\|clawback\|absorb.*refund\|negative balance" app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx -> zero hits. grep -n "insufficient\|negative.*balance" lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts -> only the code-comment acknowledgment at line 214, no policy branch or documented fallback.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the technical failure is caught (the Stripe call won't silently succeed-but-not-move-money), but the business policy for what happens to the customer and the salon afterward is undecided and unwritten.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md under a new marketplace-trust topic, cross-referenced from ToS §5.4/§5.5
findings.enforcement: checklist/doc-only at this scale (28 salons, an owner who can manually reconcile a rare edge case); becomes a code gate (auto-deduct from next payout) once weekly refund-after-payout incidents exceed roughly 1 per week

findings.title: No customer-initiated review edit or delete path exists, and no written policy states whether one should
findings.principle: State in the ToS (or a shorter reviews policy) whether a customer may edit or delete their own posted review, and for how long after posting, and build exactly that -- not silence. If the decision is 'no self-service edit, contact support,' say that explicitly so the support inbox isn't the only place a customer discovers the limitation.
findings.why: Every review platform users have encountered (Google, Yelp, Fresha) lets the author edit or remove their own review; the total absence of that control, undocumented, reads as either an oversight or a hidden retention tactic once a customer notices, either of which damages trust more than a clearly-stated 'reviews are permanent once posted' rule would.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/reviews/route.ts (POST, the only customer-facing write route) has no companion PATCH/DELETE; app/api/reviews/[id]/flag, /respond, and /photos exist but none allow the original author to edit the rating or comment text. app/api/admin/reviews/[id]/route.ts (PATCH/DELETE) is admin-only (checks profile.role==='admin' at line 25/91). app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §7.2 (lines 215-229) covers only removal BY solen.ch, never mentions the author's own edit/delete rights.
findings.absence_proof: find app/api/reviews -name 'route.ts' -> route.ts, my-booking, eligibility, featured, salon/[salon_id], [id]/flag, [id]/respond, [id]/photos -- no [id]/route.ts with a customer-authorized PATCH/DELETE. grep -in "edit.*review\|delete.*own.*review\|Bewertung.*bearbeiten" app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx -> zero hits.
findings.existing_coverage: none: the ToS covers salon-initiated flagging and solen.ch-initiated removal, but is silent on the reviewer's own rights over their own content.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx §7.2 (add a sentence) + a small [id] PATCH/DELETE route scoped to review.user_id === auth user, time-boxed if desired
findings.enforcement: doc-only decision first (owner picks a policy), then a straightforward ownership-checked route if the answer is 'yes, allow it'

findings.title: No per-user-per-salon review volume floor: automod catches cross-account bursts but not one account posting many reviews
findings.principle: Independent of the existing cross-account fraud rules, cap how many reviews a single account may post for the same salon inside a rolling window (a sensible default: no more than one new review per salon per customer per 30 days, since a real repeat customer rarely gets a second haircut within a month), and flag anything beyond that for the same moderation queue automod already writes to.
findings.why: The current review-eligibility check (one review per completed booking) is correct as a floor, but it means a customer who repeatedly books the salon's cheapest trivial service can legitimately rack up many 'verified' reviews for the same salon in a short window, inflating its rating with technically-real-booking but practically-manufactured signal. automod.ts's burst rules explicitly key on NEW ACCOUNTS clustering (3+ five-star reviews from accounts created in the last 48h) and would not catch one older, real account doing this deliberately or on a salon's behalf.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/reviews/eligibility/route.ts:16-53 only checks 'does this specific completed booking already have a review,' with no salon-level frequency check across a user's booking history. lib/automod.ts:60-113 (rules 4 and 5, the only volume-based fraud checks) both filter explicitly on `newAccounts` created within the last 48 hours, so an established account is invisible to this check regardless of how many reviews it posts for one salon.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "count\|frequency\|per.*month\|rolling" app/api/reviews/eligibility/route.ts lib/automod.ts -> no per-user-per-salon frequency logic found in either file; automod's only volume signal is the new-account-cluster rule.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: automod.ts covers a different fraud shape (coordinated fake accounts) well; this is a distinct, uncovered shape (one real account, repeat manufactured signal).
findings.enforcement: gate: automod.ts checkReview() queries reviews for (user_id, salon_id) in the trailing 30 days and flags (not hides) anything beyond the first

findings.title: No duplicate/fake-listing detection at salon onboarding: no uniqueness check on phone or address
findings.principle: At salon creation, check whether the submitted phone number or address already matches an existing salon row and surface a warning (not necessarily a hard block, since legitimate multi-location chains exist via salon_groups) to the admin approval queue rather than silently allowing an identical listing through.
findings.why: A marketplace's core promise is that each listing represents a real, distinct business. Without any duplicate check, nothing stops the same person from creating multiple salon accounts (to farm multiple sets of reviews, game search ranking, or route around a suspension by re-registering under a new email), and the admin approving each one has no signal that would reveal it.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/salons/route.ts:673-700 (the salon-creation INSERT) generates a random slug and writes the row directly; there is no SELECT checking for an existing salon with the same phone or address before the insert, and no unique constraint on either column was found in the migrations grep.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "duplicate\|existing.*salon\|already.*registered" app/api/salons/route.ts -> zero hits in the POST handler. grep -rn "UNIQUE.*address\|UNIQUE.*phone" supabase/migrations/*.sql -> zero hits (the only UNIQUE-flagged column found in a related grep was barber_walkin_queue.tracking_token, unrelated).
findings.existing_coverage: none in code; salon_groups (the multi-location chain feature) exists as the legitimate exception this check would need to account for, which is precisely why a hard block is the wrong shape and a soft admin-facing warning is the right one.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/salons/route.ts (POST handler) + admin approve queue UI
findings.enforcement: gate: before insert, query salons for phone=X OR (address similarity above a threshold) and attach a 'possible duplicate of <id>' flag the admin sees on the approval screen; never auto-reject

findings.title: A resolved bank-side chargeback never updates the booking's own payment/dispute state, so an in-app refund appeal for the same booking can proceed unaware
findings.principle: When a Stripe chargeback (charge.dispute.closed) resolves against a booking, the webhook handler must also write that outcome onto the booking itself (payment_status and/or a linked booking_disputes row), not only adjust the salon's payout ledger, so any parallel in-app refund/appeal flow for the same booking can see it happened and refuse a duplicate action.
findings.why: The two refund channels (in-app appeal via booking_disputes, and a customer going straight to their bank) are handled by genuinely well-engineered, separate, idempotent code paths, but they don't know about each other. A customer could win a bank chargeback and, independently, have an in-app refund appeal sitting open or later opened for the same booking; nothing in the current code cross-references them, so the booking's own payment_status can end up stuck out of sync with reality, and a salon could end up double-scrutinized (or, in an edge case Stripe's own accounting doesn't fully prevent, double-refunded in spirit even if not in raw Stripe dollars).
findings.local_evidence: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts case 'charge.dispute.closed' (starting line 645) decrements the payout ledger on a lost dispute via a CAS marker (lost_dispute_id), per its own detailed comment, but the comment explicitly frames this as adjusting `salon_payouts`, not `bookings.payment_status` or `booking_disputes.status`. No code was found that checks an existing booking_disputes row's status against a live Stripe dispute before allowing a salon or admin to approve/reject an in-app refund for the same booking_id.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n "booking_disputes\|payment_status" app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (lines 645-750, the dispute.closed branch) -> the branch updates salon_payouts and audit_log only; no reference to booking_disputes or a bookings.payment_status write was found inside that specific case block.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the individual money-movement mechanics on both sides (issueRefund's CAS claim, the dispute-closed ledger CAS) are each independently well-guarded against double-execution within their own channel; the cross-channel reconciliation between the two channels is the missing piece.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (dispute.closed case) + a check inside the booking_disputes salon-review / admin-action routes
findings.enforcement: gate: dispute.closed on 'lost' also sets a bookings.chargeback_status field (or reuses payment_status='refunded'), and the booking_disputes review-action route rejects an approve/reject when that field is already set, returning a clear 'already resolved via chargeback' error
